added_claim_errors: "the carryover only happens if you're still employed and still enrolled in the FSA in the new plan year": the enrollment condition is plan-dependent (the key leaves it open), so stating it as a universal rule overstates it
"If you change jobs, the whole balance — carryover included — is gone": leaves out the COBRA exception for the health FSA (Notice 2013-71)
Table labels the $680 carryover as the "best case", but a grace period covering March would save all $1,900, which A itself admits a few lines later

"Is my full $1,900 available now? Under the uniform-coverage rule it should be ... you can spend it before it's fully funded": muddled, since uniform coverage applies to the annual election from day one and the $1,900 is a leftover balance already available; it also misses the actual use of the rule, the 2027 election
"you usually have until March–April to submit receipts": run-out periods vary by plan; generic and unverifiable, though hedged with "usually"

reasons: Both answers correct the FSA-vs-HSA premise at the start, give the correct $680 cap for 2026 and the $1,220 figure, say a plan cannot have both features, and list sensible eligible expenses. B covers all three branches cleanly: it says the plan can set a lower cap, gives a grace period of up to 2.5 months (generally to March 15), and says the full $1,900 is at risk with neither feature. It also warns explicitly against prepaying in December for March dental work, which A never mentions. A treats carryover as the default ("best case ~$680"), handles the grace-period and neither-feature branches only loosely, and states plan-dependent conditions (still enrolled next year) as universal rules. Neither answer points to the 2027 open-enrollment election for the March work.
